books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

stimulus.source_note: Abraham Lincoln, First Inaugural Address, March 4, 1861. Public domain. Wording verified against the Teaching American History text (teachingamericanhistory.org/document/first-inaugural-address-6/) and the Senate document (govinfo.gov, S. Doc. 62-439). The two passages appear in this order in the address; '. . .' marks omitted text.
stimulus.text:
Apprehension seems to exist among the people of the Southern States that by the accession of a Republican Administration their property and their peace and personal security are to be endangered. There has never been any reasonable cause for such apprehension. . . . I do but quote from one of those speeches when I declare that “I have no purpose, directly or indirectly, to interfere with the institution of slavery in the States where it exists. I believe I have no lawful right to do so, and I have no inclination to do so.”

. . .

In your hands, my dissatisfied fellow-countrymen, and not in mine, is the momentous issue of civil war. The Government will not assail you. You can have no conflict without being yourselves the aggressors. . . . We are not enemies, but friends. We must not be enemies. Though passion may have strained, it must not break our bonds of affection. The mystic chords of memory . . . will yet swell the chorus of the Union, when again touched, as surely they will be, by the better angels of our nature.

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: In the first passage, Lincoln promises the Southern states that he will not do which of the following?

options.text: Interfere with slavery in the states where it already exists
Enforce the laws of the United States
options.misconception: The passage promises to leave slavery alone; enforcing the laws is what Lincoln says he will do, not what he gives up.

options.text: Collect duties and imposts in Southern ports
options.misconception: The passage says nothing about duties or ports; that pledge comes later in the address.

options.text: Allow new states to enter the Union as slave states
options.misconception: The passage is about slavery where it already exists, not about new states.

rationales.A: Lincoln quotes his own words: he has “no purpose, directly or indirectly, to interfere with the institution of slavery in the States where it exists.”
rationales.B: The passage promises to leave slavery alone; enforcing the laws is what Lincoln says he will do, not what he gives up.
rationales.C: The passage says nothing about duties or ports; that pledge comes later in the address.
rationales.D: The passage is about slavery where it already exists, not about new states.
rationales.general:
1. Lincoln names the Southern fear first: a Republican president endangering their property and peace.
2. He answers it with a direct quote from his own speeches.
3. The quote draws a line: slavery where it exists is safe from him.
4. The promise is narrow, and its narrowness matters.
Remember: when a speaker quotes himself, read the exact boundary he draws.
